transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Doc... I guess I'm here because I did something recently that really just didn't sit right with me. 

You see, I run a fairly large company. Built it from the ground up, actually. I didn't even finish junior high—just went straight to work as a kid—and I learned early on that the secret to a good business is how you treat your people. I've always prided myself on being a fair boss, a steady hand, you know? I'm the guy who keeps his cool when the supply chain breaks or the market takes a dive. I'm the one keeping everyone else calm. 

But... well, a few days ago, we were on this big board call. Standard stuff, just going over the quarter. And one of the guys asks this tiny, completely normal question about the facility budget. Just a minor line-item thing, nothing that should have even raised my blood pressure. And I... I just snapped. I mean, I completely bit his head off right there on the line in front of everybody. Just tore into him over absolutely nothing. 

And I hung up the phone after the meeting and just sat there in my office thinking, what the hell was that? Because that is not how I run my company. That is absolutely not how I treat people. Never have. It's been eating at me all week, honestly, because I just don't know where that kind of reaction came from. I can't be flying off the handle over a warehouse heating bill when hundreds of people are relying on me to steer the ship, you know? It really rattled me.
Has this kind of reaction happened to you before, or was it a one-time incident?

No, no, never. That’s exactly why I’m sitting in this chair right now, Doc. If I was the kind of guy who just went around yelling at people all the time, I probably wouldn’t have thought twice about it, right? I mean, there are plenty of bosses out there like that. Guys who think fear is a management tool. 

But I learned way back when I was just sweeping warehouse floors—because like I said, I started working full-time when I was fourteen, didn't even see the inside of a high school—I learned right then and there that you don't get good work out of people by screaming at them. You just make them hide their mistakes. So I made a promise to myself when I started hiring my own crew, building my own thing, that I’d always be the calmest guy in the room. And for thirty-something years, I really have been. 

I mean, we went through the recession in '08, we had a massive roof collapse in our main distribution center back in '14, and I didn't even raise my voice then. Millions of dollars on the line, and I just rolled up my sleeves, got everybody a cup of coffee, and said, 'Alright, how do we fix this?' That's how you handle things. 

So, no... I've never snapped like that before. Usually, if a guy messes up a budget line, I pull him aside later, we look at the spreadsheet together, and we figure it out. For me to just bark at him like a junkyard dog right there on a conference call... it was completely out of left field. Just this one time, just out of the blue, over a heating bill of all things. It hasn't happened since, and it's never happened before. Just this one single incident, and it completely threw me because it's just... it's just not who I am.
Has this incident affected your relationships with your employees or your ability to perform your job duties since it happened?

Well, that's the thing, Doc. That's really the crux of why I picked up the phone to make this appointment. I mean, I'm still working. I'm still going into the office every day, sitting in the big chair, looking at the reports. I haven't missed a day of work. But... am I really doing my job? That's the question I've been wrestling with all week. 

Because ever since that call, I've just been... second-guessing myself. Constantly. Like, there was a decision I needed to make on Tuesday about expanding the loading dock at the south facility. Normally? I look at the numbers, I talk to the site manager, I make the call in ten minutes. Boom, done, let's move forward. But this time... I just kept looking at the paperwork. I kept thinking, 'What if I miss something? What if I misread the budget and snap at somebody again?' So I put it off. I told them we'd revisit it next week. And then yesterday, there was a vendor dispute I would usually mediate myself, just get both guys on the phone and hash it out. Instead, I handed it off to my VP of Operations. I just told him, 'You handle this one, I've got too much on my plate.' Which wasn't true. I just didn't trust myself to get on that call and stay level-headed. 

And my employees... they're professionals, they're not going to say anything to my face. But I can see it. I can see the way my assistant hesitates before she brings me a file now. I can see the guys on the floor giving me a slightly wider berth when I walk through the warehouse. And that breaks my heart, honestly. Because my entire leadership style, my whole philosophy for the last thirty-some years, has been built on trust and approachability. If my people are afraid to bring me a problem, then the company is in danger. 

So yeah, I'm technically still at the helm, but... I'm leaning heavily on my executive team for things I should be doing myself. I'm delaying calls, I'm avoiding decisions about the facilities, and it's all because that one blow-up made me realize that whatever is going on with me right now, it's starting to affect my judgment. And as a CEO, if you can't trust your own judgment, you've got nothing. So it's definitely impacting how I'm running things, even if the bottom line hasn't shown it yet. I just can't have my people walking on eggshells around me, Doc. It's not right.
Have you been feeling anxious or on edge most of the time since the incident?

Anxious? On edge? Yeah... yeah, Doc, I'd say that hits the nail right on the head. It's like my whole body is just wound up tight, like one of those cheap pocket watches you overwind and you can just feel the gears straining, you know? 

I sit there at my desk—and I've got this big, heavy mahogany desk, beautiful piece of furniture I bought back when we opened our third warehouse, really anchors the room—and I try to just look at a simple spreadsheet or read an email. But I just can't settle into the chair. My shoulders are practically up to my ears all day. And the worst part, the part that really makes me feel like I'm losing my grip a little, is how jumpy I am. 

I mean, if a door shuts hard out in the hallway, or... or even if the big laser printer just kicks on behind me to print out a manifest, I practically jump out of my skin. I jump like something went off again. Just this massive jolt right through my chest, like a shock of electricity. And then I'm sitting there, alone in my office, and I have to put my pen down or take my hands off the keyboard because it takes me a few minutes just to get my hands steady. 

My hands are literally shaking over a printer noise, Doc. I've worked in loud warehouses my whole life. I grew up around forklifts dropping heavy pallets, delivery trucks backing up, metal clanging against metal on the loading docks... none of that ever bothered me. I could sleep through a freight train going by. But now? A door clicks shut a little too loud and I'm sitting there vibrating for five minutes trying to catch my breath. It's exhausting, honestly, just being this... this on guard all day long. I've never felt anything like it.
Have you been having any recurring, intrusive thoughts since the incident?

Thoughts? Yeah... yeah, I guess you could call them that. But it feels more like... well, it’s like a bad film that I didn't ask to see, you know? A movie somebody just forces you to watch when you're trying to do something else. 

I'll be sitting there, just doing the mundane stuff I've done ten thousand times to keep this company running. I'll be right in the middle of a call with the regional managers, or maybe I'm just sitting quiet, looking at the numbers—tracing my pen down the budget columns, trying to figure out where we can trim the fat for the next quarter. And then, out of nowhere, the blast and that fire by the loading area just jump back into my head. 

Just... boom. Right there behind my eyes. It's not even like I'm trying to remember it. I'm actively trying *not* to. But I can see the flames going up the side of the corrugated metal, I can see the whole mess at the loading dock, and it completely derails me. One second I'm looking at a spreadsheet or talking about freight costs, and the next I'm just staring blankly at the wall, seeing that fire all over again. 

I have to literally shake my head, like a dog shaking off water, just to get back to reality. And the guys on the phone, they'll be sitting there saying, 'Boss? You still there? We lose you?' And I have to clear my throat and pretend I was just reviewing a file or reading an email. But really, my mind was miles away, stuck right back at that loading area watching it burn. It just plays on a loop, Doc. I can't seem to shut the projector off, no matter how hard I try to focus on the work in front of me.
Have you been avoiding certain places, people, or activities since the incident?

Yeah, I have. And I hate to admit it, because it makes me feel like I'm hiding, but... yeah, I definitely have. 

For one thing, I've been completely keeping away from the new building. Which is just ridiculous, honestly, because I’m the one who spearheaded that whole expansion project. Before all this happened, I was over there three, maybe four times a week. I'd walk the site, shoot the breeze with the contractors, check the progress on the framing... I loved watching it come together, it's a huge milestone for the company. But now? I haven't set foot near the place. I haven't even driven past it. I actually take a completely different exit off the interstate in the mornings, which adds about fifteen minutes to my commute, just so I don't have to see the roofline from the highway. I just... I can't go over there right now. I can't do it.

And it's not even just the physical places, Doc, it's the paperwork, too. It's following me right into my office. Right there on the corner of that big mahogany desk I was telling you about, there's a stack of files I desperately need to review. The mortgage folder for the new site, the quarterly safety reports... they're just sitting there. Completely unopened. They've been sitting there for days. 

Every morning I come in, I pour my coffee, I sit down in my chair, and I tell myself, 'Alright, you're the boss, do your job, open the damn files.' But I swear to you, the minute I actually reach my hand out for them... my stomach just drops. It completely falls out from under me. It's exactly like when you go over the top of a steep hill on a roller coaster, or when you hit a bad patch of turbulence on a flight—just this sudden, sickening plunge right in my gut. So I pull my hand back. I tell myself I'll get to it after lunch, and then after lunch I tell my assistant I'll do it tomorrow. I have never ignored a safety report in my thirty years of running this business. Never. But right now, just the thought of touching those folders makes me feel physically sick.
Are you having trouble sleeping or experiencing any changes in your appetite since the incident?

Sleep? Appetite? Honestly, Doc, I haven't really noticed any big changes there. I mean, I'm a big guy, you know? I've always had a healthy appetite. My wife, she makes this incredible pot roast on Sundays—slow cooks it all day with the carrots and the little red potatoes, the whole house smells like it by noon—and I'm still putting away my usual portion, maybe even going back for seconds. Same with lunch. I've got this deli down the street from the main office, Sal's, been going there since we opened the second warehouse back in '98. I still get my turkey and provolone on rye every Tuesday and Thursday, just like clockwork. The guys at the counter see me walk in and they've already got the slicer going. So, no, the food thing hasn't been an issue. I'm still eating just fine, maybe even looking forward to meals just to have a break from sitting at that mahogany desk trying not to look at those safety files. 

And as for sleep... well, I've never been one of those guys who needs eight hours anyway. Never have been. Even back when I was a kid, growing up with four brothers in a house with one bathroom, you learned to get by on what you could. I usually hit the mattress around eleven, maybe watch a little of the late news just to see what the weather's doing for the freight routes the next day, and I'm up by five-thirty. That hasn't really changed. I'm still getting my solid six hours. I mean, sure, I'm exhausted during the day, like I said before, from being so tense and jumpy all the time. By three o'clock I feel like I've run a marathon just sitting in my chair. But when I actually put my head on the pillow? No, I'm out pretty quick. I don't lay there tossing and turning or staring at the ceiling or anything. So I guess, in the grand scheme of things, my eating and sleeping are about the only things that feel normal right now.
Have you been having any repetitive behaviors or mental acts that you feel driven to perform since the incident?

Repetitive behaviors? Like... like having to flip a light switch a certain number of times or wash my hands over and over? No, no, nothing like that. I know a guy, actually, a supplier up in Albany, who does that sort of thing. Great guy, runs a tight ship, but if you go to his office, he's got this whole routine with his coffee cup before he can sit down to look at a purchase order. Taps it three times on the saucer, always three times. 

But for me? No, I haven't noticed anything like that. I mean, sure, I've got my routines, right? I've been running this company for thirty years, you don't get to be the chief executive without a little structure. I always check the warehouse floor before I go up to my office, always walk the perimeter of the main lot before I leave for the day. But that's just good management, you know? That's just keeping an eye on the investment. It's not something I feel... driven to do because of the fire. It's just how I operate. 

And as far as mental acts... I don't even really know what that means, to be honest. Like counting in my head or something? No, my head's too full of everything else to be counting anything. Like I said, I'm just trying to keep the bad movie from playing in my head when I'm trying to work. I'm not sitting there reciting the alphabet backwards or anything to make it stop. I just shake it off and try to get back to the spreadsheets. So, yeah, I'd have to say no on that one, Doc. Just the usual day-to-day stuff I've always done.
Are there any specific thoughts or memories related to the incident that you've been trying to avoid thinking about?

Specific thoughts or memories I'm trying to avoid? Well... no. Not really. I mean, I know I just spent ten minutes telling you how I can't drive past the new building or open those safety files, but that's different. That's stuff out there in the world. But my own thoughts? No, I'm not really doing that. 

You gotta understand, Doc, I'm not the kind of guy who hides from his own brain. I think I mentioned it before, but I didn't exactly take the traditional route to the CEO chair. I actually dropped out of school halfway through the eighth grade. Eighth grade! Most kids my age were complaining about homework or whatever, and I was out hauling scrap metal and sweeping warehouse floors for fifty cents an hour just to help my old man pay the heating bill. When you grow up like that, and you build a company like mine from absolute scratch, you learn pretty quick that you can't run away from what's in your head. If there's a problem, you look at it. You figure it out. You don't get to be the boss by burying your head in the sand every time you remember a bad day.

So, no, I'm not sitting around trying to block out specific memories of the... the incident. It's not like I'm sitting in my office saying, 'Oh, don't think about the smoke,' or 'Don't think about the sirens.' I'm not doing that. Like I said before, the memories just sort of pop up on their own, like a bad movie playing in the background while I'm trying to look at my spreadsheets. But I'm not actively trying to shove the thoughts away or dodge certain parts of what happened. I just... I just want to get my work done, you know? I've got three hundred employees relying on me to make payroll next Friday, so I don't have the luxury of sitting around playing hide-and-seek with my own memories. If the thought comes, it comes. I just grit my teeth, take a breath, and try to look back down at the balance sheet. So no, I wouldn't say I'm trying to avoid any specific thoughts about it.
Are you finding it harder to connect with your family or friends since this incident happened?

Well, connecting... I mean, I'm still around them, you know? I haven't locked myself in the basement or anything. I'm still showing up. But it’s... it’s different. I mentioned my wife earlier, right? The Sunday dinners, the pot roast. Usually, sitting down with her at the end of the day or on a weekend, that’s my anchor. That’s what makes all the seventy-hour work weeks and the stress of running a company worth it. But lately, I’m sitting there at the dining table, and she’s talking about her garden or what the grandkids are up to, and it just feels... flat. 

And it’s not just with people, either, it’s... well, it’s the things I do just to settle myself down. Like, I’ve got this beautiful wooden chess set in my study. Hand-carved, bought it up in upstate New York maybe fifteen, twenty years ago. I’ve always loved sitting down with a good chess problem. Setting up the board, working through the strategy, trying to see five moves ahead. It’s a quiet thing, but it settles my mind. That, or going through my hiking notes. I keep these really detailed logs, you see, of all the trails I’ve done over the years—mileage, elevation, what the weather was doing, how the boots held up. I usually get a real kick out of reviewing them, planning out the next trip up to the mountains, just getting lost in the details of it. 

But right now? I look at the chessboard, or I open up my hiking journals, or I'm sitting right there having a beautiful dinner with my wife, and... nothing. Things that usually settle me, like a chess problem, my hiking notes, or dinner with my wife, just feel completely flat right now. It’s the strangest thing, Doc, because I know I should enjoy them. I know I love my wife, I know I love chess, I know I'm supposed to be having a good time. But I just can't get there. It's like I'm going through the motions of enjoying my life, but the actual feeling of it is just... it's just not showing up.
Do you feel guilty about how you reacted during the conference call?

Guilty? Yeah. Yeah, Doc, I do. Honestly, it’s eating at me. I mean, that’s... that’s the whole reason I’m sitting in this chair talking to you today. I came in because I snapped on that board call, and I mean, I really snapped. 

It was over nothing, too. Just a... a small, completely standard question about the facility budget. One of the board members—a guy I've known for probably fifteen years, good guy, always does his due diligence—he just asked for a minor clarification on a line item for the facility's maintenance fund for the next quarter. Just standard, routine stuff. The kind of question I’ve answered a thousand times in my sleep, right? You pull up the spreadsheet, you read the number, you move on. 

But instead of just giving him the figure, I just... I bit his head off. I raised my voice, I got incredibly defensive, and I basically told him he was wasting my time and questioning my competence, right there in front of everyone else on the line. There was just this dead silence on the call afterward. You could have heard a pin drop. 

And I realized right then, sitting there in that silence... that is just not how I run my company. It is absolutely not how I treat people. You don't build a business from scratch, hauling scrap as an eighth-grade dropout, by treating your partners and your people like garbage when they're just trying to do their jobs. My whole leadership philosophy for thirty years has been about respect. You respect the guy sweeping the warehouse floor, and you respect the guy signing the checks. You keep a level head. 

So to lose my temper like that, to just explode over a simple budget question... yeah, I feel terrible about it. It’s embarrassing, quite frankly. It shook me up enough to make me pick up the phone and make this appointment, because I can't be acting like that. I've got three hundred people looking to me to keep this ship steered straight, and I can't do that if I'm barking at them over pennies.
Are you having any thoughts that keep repeating in your mind and feel like you can't control them?

Yeah, well, like I was touching on a minute ago... it's exactly that. I mean, I'll be sitting there at my desk—it's this big, solid mahogany desk, by the way, bought it at an estate auction twenty years ago when the company finally turned our first real, sustainable profit—and I'll be right in the middle of a very important call. Or maybe I'm just reviewing the quarterly projections, really drilling down into the numbers, because with the supply chain the way it is right now, you really have to watch every single penny if you want to keep the lights on and keep everyone employed. So I'm looking at these numbers, completely focused on the business, and then... it just happens. 

The blast. The memory of it, and then that massive fire breaking out right by the loading area... it all just jumps back into my head. Like I said before, it's exactly like a bad film I didn't ask to see. It just starts playing right over whatever I'm trying to look at. 

And it's incredibly frustrating, Doc, because I'm a guy who fixes things. If a forklift breaks down, I get a mechanic. If a client is unhappy, I get on a plane and go shake their hand. I control my environment. But this? I'll be staring at a column of figures, trying to calculate our overhead, and my brain just hijacks me. I'm suddenly right back at that loading area, seeing the flames, and I can't just reach up and hit the off switch. I just have to sit there, maybe pretend I'm listening to whatever the guy on the conference line is saying, and wait for the movie to finish so I can get back to my numbers. It's completely out of my hands, and frankly, I absolutely hate that feeling.
Are you finding it harder to perform your job or interact with others at work since the incident happened?

Well... yes and no. I mean, I'm still showing up. I’m still pulling into my parking spot at 6:30 AM sharp, grabbing my coffee, and sitting at my desk just like I have every single workday for the last thirty years. I haven't taken a day off. So, I'm still technically working. 

But as for actually performing the job... it’s, well, it's getting complicated. Take the facility itself, for instance. After something like that happens, there are a hundred decisions that need to be made, right away. You've got insurance adjusters, contractors, structural engineers wanting to look at the damage by the loading area. Normally, I’d be right out there in the thick of it. I’d be walking the site, pointing out what needs fixing first, negotiating the repair costs directly with the foremen. I'm a hands-on guy, Doc. I built this business from nothing, I don't just pass off major facility repairs. 

But right now? I keep putting those decisions off. There’s a stack of estimates sitting right there on my desk, and every time I look at them, I just find an excuse to go do something else. I'm delaying making any real calls about the facility. In fact, I'm leaning heavily on my VP of Operations to handle the contractor calls and the walk-throughs—things I would normally handle myself without a second thought. I just tell him, 'You handle it, let me know what they say,' and I shut my door. 

And that’s... that’s what really scares me, to be perfectly honest with you. Between hiding from the contractors and that whole mess on the board call I told you about... it really made me stop and take a hard look in the mirror. Because snapping at a guy who's just doing his due diligence, and avoiding the very decisions that keep the building standing... it made me realize this is actually starting to affect my judgment. It's affecting my leadership. And when you're the chief executive, when you've got three hundred people relying on your judgment to keep a roof over their heads, you can't afford to be off your game like this. You just can't. So, I'm in the building, sure, but I'm not leading the way I'm supposed to.
Are you finding it difficult to fulfill your responsibilities as a CEO due to the way you've been feeling since the incident?

Well, yeah, that’s... that’s exactly what I was just getting at, Doc. I know I'm probably repeating myself a bit here, but that is the exact heart of the matter. 

I mean, I’m still technically working, sure. I’m physically in the building, my name is on the door, I'm signing the essential paperwork. But as far as actually fulfilling the real responsibilities of a chief executive? It’s... it’s slipping. Like I was just saying about the facility repairs. I am actively delaying making any real decisions about fixing up that area. Normally, I’d be out there with a hard hat myself, haggling with the contractors over the price of materials, because you don't build a profitable business by just writing blank checks to the first guy who gives you an estimate. But now? I'm just leaning entirely on my VP of Operations to handle all those calls and walk-throughs. I’m delegating things I would normally never delegate, things I’ve handled myself without breaking a sweat for thirty years. I just can't bring myself to deal with it.

And then, you know, you combine that avoidance with what happened on that board call I told you about... that was the moment it really hit me. That reaction, losing my temper and snapping at a guy for absolutely no reason, it made me realize this whole thing is genuinely starting to affect my judgment. It’s compromising my leadership. And that’s the one thing I can't afford to lose. If the CEO's judgment goes, if I can't be trusted to keep a level head or make the tough calls on facility maintenance, the whole company feels it. Three hundred families rely on me to steer this ship. So, yes, to answer your question, it is becoming incredibly difficult to do my job the way I know it needs to be done, and frankly, it's terrifying me.
Are you feeling like you're unable to be yourself around others, including your family, friends, or employees, since this incident happened?

Well, it’s funny you phrase it like that... unable to be myself. Because, honestly, sometimes lately I don't even feel like I'm in my own skin. 

Take my home setup, for example. I’ve got this office at the house—my wife set it up for me a few years back, got this nice heavy oak desk, some good solid bookshelves, because I end up taking a lot of evening calls. You know, dealing with the West Coast distributors or the overseas freight guys, because business doesn't just stop at five o'clock just because you want to eat dinner. So I'll be sitting there, in my own house, on one of these calls... and it is the strangest damn thing, Doc. 

I'll be right in the middle of talking, making a point about a contract, and suddenly the whole room just... it looks distant. Like it's stretching away from me, or like I'm looking at my own office through the wrong end of a pair of binoculars. And my own voice... I can hear myself speaking, I know I'm the one laying down the law on shipping rates, but it sounds completely strange to me. It’s almost like I'm watching myself talk instead of being fully there in the chair. Like I'm just a spectator floating somewhere behind my own head, watching this guy do my job. 

And how are you supposed to be yourself around your people, or even your family, when you get off a call and you feel like you weren't even the one talking? I’ve always been a grounded guy. I know who I am, I know exactly where my feet are planted. But having to sit there and blink a few times just to feel like I'm back in my own body before I walk into the kitchen to see my wife... it just makes no sense to me. I've never been a flaky person, I don't get my head in the clouds. But this feeling of just not being fully there... it makes me feel completely disconnected from everything I'm trying to hold together.
Are you feeling an overwhelming urge to repeat certain actions or behaviors since the incident?

Repeat actions? Like... doing things over and over again? No, no, I can't say that I am. 

I mean, don't get me wrong, Doc, I am a creature of habit. I think anyone who runs a company this size has to be. Like I mentioned earlier, I pull into that same parking spot at 6:30 AM every single morning. I walk in, I get my coffee—black, always from the machine by the breakroom—and I sit at my desk to review the overnight shipping logs. I’ve done that exact same sequence of events for the better part of thirty years. And you know, my wife, she always jokes that you could set a Swiss watch by my morning routine. 

But that’s just discipline, you know? That’s just how you build a business from scratch when you don't have a fancy high school or college education to fall back on. You figure out what works, and you stick to it. You build a structure. So sure, I repeat my routine, but it's not some... overwhelming urge, like I'm being forced to do it by my own brain. I don't have to go back and check the office door locks five times, or tap my desk before I make a phone call, or anything strange like that. If I need to change my schedule for a morning meeting, I change it. I'm not stuck in any kind of weird loop, if that's what you're getting at. So, no, I haven't noticed anything like that at all.
Are you finding it difficult to enjoy or participate in activities that you normally found pleasurable before this incident happened?

Well, yeah... yeah, I am. And that’s been bothering me just as much as the work stuff, to be honest. 

Because normally, I have my ways of winding down, you know? When you carry the kind of weight I do all day, you need a way to decompress, otherwise you’d just burn out. For me, it’s always been a few specific things. Like, I’ve got this old chessboard set up in the study. I don't really play against anyone, but I like to work through these classic chess problems. It’s quiet, it’s logical, it makes sense. Or I’ll pull out my old hiking notes. I used to do a lot of trails up in the mountains, and I’ve kept these detailed logs of routes and gear and weather conditions for years. Going over them, planning out hypothetical trips... it usually settles my mind right down.

And then, of course, there’s dinner with my wife. We’ve been married thirty-two years, Doc. Every night, no matter what kind of fire I’ve had to put out at the plant, sitting down at the table with her, having a good meal, talking about her day... that’s my anchor. That’s the part of the day I always look forward to. 

But lately? Since all this happened? It’s just... flat. That’s the only word for it. I sit down at the chessboard, and I’m just staring at pieces of wood. There’s no satisfaction in figuring out the move. I open my hiking logs, and it just looks like a bunch of meaningless scribbles on paper. I don't feel that little spark of excitement I usually get. And even dinner with my wife... I’m sitting there across from the woman I love, eating a meal she made, and I know in my head that I should be happy. I know I should be enjoying that time with her. But I just can't get there. The feeling just won't come. It’s like the part of my brain that actually enjoys things has just been switched off, and I’m just going through the motions waiting for it to click back on. And it just isn't happening.
Are you feeling an overwhelming need to perform specific rituals or behaviors to relieve anxiety or stress?

Rituals? To relieve anxiety? No, no, I wouldn't say that. It sounds kind of like what you were asking a minute ago about repeating things, right? 

I mean, look, Doc, I have my ways of dealing with stress, sure. When you're the chief executive of a company, and you've got hundreds of employees relying on you to make sure their paychecks clear every Friday, you have to have a way to manage the pressure. If you didn't, your head would explode. But it's not like I'm... I don't know, washing my hands twenty times or counting the tiles on the ceiling or anything like that. 

When I get stressed, I just fall back on what I know. Like I was saying about my routines. If things are going sideways at the plant—say, a supplier falls through or a machine goes down—I don't start doing some weird ritual. I just get to work. I know who I am, I know exactly where my feet are planted. But having to sit there and blink a few times just to feel like I'm back in my own body before I walk into the kitchen to see my wife... it just makes no sense to me. I've never been a flaky person, I don't get my head in the clouds.
